assessment:
This manuscript by Kamadurai et al. addresses a fundamental question in ubiquitin biology: how do HECT E3 ligases transfer ubiquitin from their active site cysteine to substrate lysines? The authors set out to define the structural and mechanistic basis for the second step of HECT-mediated ubiquitination—the ligation of ubiquitin from the E3~Ub intermediate to substrate. This work is significant because, despite the importance of HECT E3s in numerous cellular processes and disease states, the mechanisms underlying substrate ubiquitination have remained poorly understood due to the absence of structures representing E3~Ub-substrate complexes.

The key achievement of this study is the determination of a 3.1 Å crystal structure of the yeast HECT E3 Rsp5 with its active site simultaneously crosslinked to both ubiquitin and a substrate peptide (Sna3C). To obtain this structure, the authors developed an innovative three-way crosslinking strategy using click chemistry to stabilize the otherwise transient catalytic intermediate. The structure reveals that ubiquitin is sandwiched between the HECT domain N- and C-lobes, with the C-lobe and ubiquitin rotated approximately 130° relative to their orientation during E2-to-E3 transfer. This architecture is stabilized by extensive three-way interactions involving the N-lobe, C-lobe, and covalently linked ubiquitin, particularly anchored by ubiquitin's Arg74. The authors complement the structural data with comprehensive alanine scanning mutagenesis of 180 surface residues in the HECT domain, which maps mutations affecting ligation to surfaces distinct from those affecting E2-to-E3 transfer, supporting the existence of a specific catalytic architecture for ligation. Substrate selection assays demonstrate that the fixed HECT domain architecture restricts substrate lysine positioning, requiring approximately 10 residues between the WW domain-binding PPXY motif and the acceptor lysine. The generality of the mechanism is supported by sequence conservation and functional data from other NEDD4-family E3s.

The evidence supporting the main conclusions is strong and multifaceted. The crystal structure provides direct visualization of the ligation-competent state, with good electron density for most regions. The alanine scan systematically validates the functional importance of structural features, with mutations at the N-lobe/C-lobe interface and in regions contacting ubiquitin specifically impairing ligation without affecting E2-to-E3 transfer. Particularly compelling are the rescue experiments showing that the defect from mutating the C-lobe's Phe806 can be complemented by introducing an aromatic residue at position 506 in the N-lobe, demonstrating the importance of interlobe interactions. Rapid quench-flow kinetic analyses provide quantitative support for the severity of defects. The substrate selection assays elegantly demonstrate that lysine positioning relative to the active site is critical, with dramatic loss of activity when the linker is reduced below 10 residues. However, some aspects remain incompletely resolved. The role of the C-terminus is unclear, as deletion impairs activity but alanine substitutions do not. The critical N-lobe loop (residues 491-495) is not visible in the structure and its precise mechanism remains speculative, though Rosetta modeling provides plausible hypotheses. The mechanism of polyubiquitination and how ubiquitin itself is positioned as an acceptor requires further investigation.

This work makes important contributions to understanding ubiquitin transfer mechanisms. It challenges the prevailing model that HECT domain lobes are flexibly tethered during ligation, instead demonstrating a specific, constrained architecture. The findings have broad implications for understanding how HECT E3s achieve substrate specificity and how different E3 families have evolved distinct strategies for ubiquitin transfer. The development of the three-way crosslinking methodology is a technical advance that may enable similar studies of other transient catalytic intermediates. The work will be of significant interest to researchers studying ubiquitin biology, E3 ligases, and post-translational modifications more broadly.
